question: A video published on Meta by Alessandro Barbero in which the Italian historian shared his opinion on an upcoming national referendum has had its visibility limited and been put behind a screen on which the words ‘False information: checked by independent fact-checkers’ are overlaid1.
Meta’s decision is far from an isolated case, and raises major concerns about the role platforms play in moderating content concerning matters of public interest.

Article 11 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights enshrines freedom of expression and information and the right to receive and impart opinions without interference, while the Digital Services Act (DSA) lays down requirements for large online platforms concerning proportionality, transparency and the upholding of pluralism, particularly as regards political and civic discourse.

In addition, Article 34 DSA requires that assessments be carried out concerning systemic threats to democratic processes and public debate. In the light of the above: Is the Commission thinking of strengthening procedural guarantees and effective remedies for users, particularly as regards academic content and civic discourse? Supporter2
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.5.2026) The Digital Services Act (DSA1) entitles recipients of hosting services to a statement of reasons, and recipients of online platforms to an internal complaint-handling system, if their content is restricted by providers of those services. It also entitles recipients to access out-ofcourt dispute settlement bodies2.

On this basis, millions of moderation decisions have been reversed since 20243. The DSA further mandates providers of very large online platforms (VLOPs4) to identify, analyse and assess systemic risks in the EU stemming from their services, and to mitigate those risks.

The Commission Guidelines on the mitigation of systemic risks for electoral processes pursuant to Article 35(3) of the DSA5 point out that collaborating with independent factcheckers who work on the basis of high ethical and professional standards can be one way for VLOPs to mitigate risks to civic discourse.

All content moderation decisions based on factchecking are subject to the transparency and redress measures mentioned above. The Commission initiated proceedings in relation to Meta for the suspected demotion of political content through Facebook and Instagram’s recommender systems6. The Commission is continuously monitoring compliance with the obligations of the DSA.

The Commission published the European Democracy Shield7, which aims at reinforcing the integrity of the information space in the EU, and where the EU’s commitment to academic freedom is reaffirmed. Pursuant to Article 91(2) of the DSA, the Commission shall evaluate the DSA by 17 November 2027, addressing, among others, its impact on the respect for the right of freedom of expression and information.
